title: Make the Conflict Smaller Before Trying to Resolve It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short piece diagnoses a common failure mode in interpersonal conflict: heated arguments tend to produce sweeping generalizations ("you never listen to me," "you always do this") that are functionally impossible to resolve because they ask one person to defend or disprove an entire history in a single accusation. The proposed fix is to deliberately narrow the conflict to a specific, describable moment before trying to resolve it — asking "what specifically happened" rather than responding to or issuing broad character judgments. The piece explains why this works psychologically: defending one's entire character triggers defensiveness, while explaining one concrete episode usually allows acknowledgment without feeling attacked. It closes by noting that shrinking a conflict doesn't excuse a larger pattern if one exists, but makes it addressable one piece at a time rather than all at once.
points: Heated conflict tends to produce sweeping generalizations ("you never listen to me") that are functionally impossible to resolve because they ask someone to defend an entire history in one sentence.
Responding to a broad accusation with an equally broad defense just escalates the fight; the fix is narrowing the conflict to one specific, describable moment.
Asking "what specifically happened" shifts the emotional tone: defending one moment feels answerable, while defending one's whole character triggers defensiveness.
Making conflict smaller doesn't excuse a larger pattern if one exists — it makes that pattern addressable one concrete piece at a time instead of all at once.
quotes: You never listen to me," "You always do this," "You don't care about anything I say," and "This is just like you" are prime examples.
Such generalizations, even when accurate, are nearly impossible to address because they ask one person to defend or disprove an entire history captured in a single accusation.
Making the conflict smaller by addressing it in the present allows both parties to be more precise and find a way forward.

When someone is asked to defend their entire character, they naturally become defensive. But when someone is asked to explain one moment or episode, they can usually acknowledge what happened without feeling attacked.
Smaller conflicts leave room for accountability because they don't demand someone confess to everything at once.
Conflicts shrink the moment they become specific. Sweeping accusations feel true when tempers are high, but they can never be resolved. They only escalate.
